prompt: Since Playwright 1.51 (last good version 1.50.1; still present in 1.61.1 and on main), a URL glob pattern for request routing that contains an explicit default port, for example http://localhost:80/** , never matches. The browser normalizes that address to http://localhost/, and the request URL that Playwright reports never contains a default port (80 for http, 443 for https). So such a route is silently dead, and the navigation fails with a connection refused error. The same happens for routing on a browser context, for waiting until the page has a given URL, and for the assertion that the page has a URL. The documentation says that a URL string pattern is resolved with the standard URL constructor, which drops default ports. The same 1.51 change also broke two other normalizations that worked in 1.50.1: a pattern with characters that the request URL shows percent-encoded (a space against %20), and internationalized host names (münchen.de against its punycode form xn--mnchen-3ya.de). The cause is a 1.51 change that replaces every part of the pattern, the host and port included, with an opaque placeholder before URL resolution, so URL normalization no longer applies to the pattern. Expected: these patterns match again, as in 1.50. The reporter suggests replacing only the parts that contain glob special characters (*, ?, {, }, backslash) and letting literal parts go through URL resolution as before. This keeps an earlier fix for question marks in patterns working.
Since 1.51, request-routing URL patterns with an explicit default port like :80, a space, or a non-ASCII host never match. Restore the 1.50 normalization.

When Playwright's HTTP request API, the request object of a browser context, follows a redirect, it updates the Host header to the host of the redirect target only if the header name is all lowercase. If the Host header was set with other casing, for example "Host" with a capital H, through the headers that a browser context adds to every request or through the headers of one request, the redirected request keeps the original Host value. A redirect from https://example.com/page to https://api.example.com/data then sends the old host, which causes connection failures or wrong routing. All other header operations in the same code compare header names without regard to case. The redirect should update the Host header whatever the casing of its name.
When Playwright's request API follows a redirect, a Host header written with uppercase letters keeps the old host instead of the new one. Please fix it.

In Playwright, finding an element by its accessibility role gives the wrong role for a search input that has a list attribute which does not point to a datalist element. Playwright treats such an input as a combobox, so a role lookup for combobox finds it and a lookup for searchbox does not. Chrome's own accessibility tree reports searchbox in these cases. Three cases show the bug: the list attribute names an id that does not exist, it names a div instead of a datalist, or it is empty. Per the HTML spec, a list attribute that does not point at a datalist means there is no suggestion source, and the HTML accessibility mapping then gives a search input the searchbox role. Only when the list attribute points at a real datalist should the input be a combobox. Text, email, telephone and URL inputs already check for a real datalist and get this right; for the search input, Playwright only checks that the attribute exists. Aria snapshot assertions and role assertions disagree with the browser and screen readers because of this. Seen in version 1.61.1 and on main.
Playwright says a search input is a combobox when its list attribute doesn't point to a real datalist, but Chrome says searchbox. Please make them match.

Regression since Playwright 1.58.2: on Android under Termux, Playwright fails with an error saying that the platform android is not supported, even when the user sets the environment variable that tells Playwright where browsers are installed. It happens both when that variable is set to 0 and when it points to an explicit folder. Steps: install the latest Playwright in Termux, set that variable, and run any Playwright command, for example the browser install command. The cause is that Playwright now works out its default per-user cache folder as soon as it loads, before it looks at the variable, and on an unsupported platform that lookup fails with the platform error. Expected: when the browser location is given through the variable, Playwright should not compute the default cache folder when it loads and should not hit the unsupported-platform check, as in earlier releases. Loading Playwright on Termux must work, so that Termux users can supply their own browser installation.
Playwright now crashes on Termux, saying the platform is not supported, even when I set the browsers location environment variable. Please make that override work again, like in 1.58.

The accessibility snapshot that Playwright produces for AI agents (both the page snapshot in the Playwright API and the snapshot tool of the Playwright MCP server) loses the accessible name of a button in one layout. The button contains an outer span. Inside it are two spans: the first holds an SVG icon marked aria-hidden="true" (also focusable="false" and tabindex="-1"), the second holds the text "Add New Item". The snapshot shows the button with no name, only its role, ref and cursor hint, instead of the button with the name "Add New Item". The name can be computed: locating the button by its role and the name "Add New Item" works, and Chromium's own full accessibility tree also gives the correct name. Because the name is missing, AI agents that navigate by the snapshot cannot tell what the button does. Expected: the snapshot lists the button with the name "Add New Item". The reporter suspects that the snapshot output does not follow the text through the nested spans when a hidden icon sits next to it, or that it computes names differently from locating by role. Seen with Playwright MCP 0.0.78 and headless Chromium on macOS.
Buttons whose label sits in nested spans next to a hidden SVG icon show up with no name in the AI accessibility snapshot. Please fix.

Playwright's browser command-line client (the one that opens a browser session and then runs actions such as a click on an element reference from the page snapshot) exits with status 0 when an action fails. Example: open https://example.com, then click an element reference that does not exist, such as e999999. The command prints an error section that says the element reference does not exist on the page, but the exit status is 0. With the option for JSON output, the JSON response marks the result as an error, and the exit status is still 0. Shell scripts, CI jobs and coding-agent shell tools use the exit status to decide whether a command succeeded, so they record the failed browser action as successful. Expected: when the final tool response of a command is marked as an error, the command exits with a non-zero status, in both the text and the JSON output modes. Seen with version 0.1.17 of the CLI package, Node.js 24, macOS.
The Playwright browser CLI exits with status 0 when an action fails, like clicking a missing element reference. Make it exit non-zero, in text and JSON mode.

When the Playwright test runner collects git information for the report on CI, the part that captures a diff against the pull request base changes the user's repository. On a pull request build where the base commit is known, it fetches that base commit from the remote with a depth limit of one. In a repository that already has its full history, the depth limit turns the clone into a shallow one: history is cut at the base commit, and the last commit of every file becomes the base commit. This state stays for the rest of the CI job. It happens during config setup, before the web server starts, so every process Playwright starts and every later CI step sees the cut history. It does not reproduce on a developer machine, because diff capture is on by default on CI and off by default locally. Example: a site generator that takes each page's last-modified date from git gives every page the same date, the date of the base commit, after the test run, with no error. Expected: collecting report metadata must not change the repository. A complete clone must still be a complete clone after the run, and the diff must still be captured. The reporter suggests not using the depth limit when the repository is not shallow, or fetching into a separate object store. The current workaround is to turn off diff capture in the git information setting. Seen in 1.61.1 and still in 1.62.1.
On CI pull request builds, Playwright's git diff capture turns my full clone into a shallow one. It should still capture the diff but leave the clone complete.

In Playwright 1.62.1 with Chromium, saving a browser context's storage with IndexedDB included leaves an IndexedDB connection open in the page that the data was read from. That open connection blocks any later delete or re-create of the database on that origin, including the one that Playwright does itself when it restores storage. Two symptoms follow. First: open a page on any origin, create a database with one object store and one record, close the database, then save the context's storage with IndexedDB included; deleting the database from the page is now reported as blocked instead of succeeding. Without the save step the delete succeeds. Second: in the same setup, restoring that saved storage into the same context while the page is still open on that origin never finishes. It does not reject, and the context's default timeout has no effect on it. Reloading the page, navigating it away, closing it, or restoring into a new context all make the restore work, and the data is then correct. Expected: saving storage closes the IndexedDB connections it opens and leaves the page as it found it, and restoring storage works whether or not pages of the context are open on that origin. If it truly cannot proceed, it should fail within the context timeout instead of hanging.
Saving browser context storage with IndexedDB leaves a database connection open, so restoring that storage later hangs forever while a page is open. Please fix it.

When a search input is embedded in the text that names another element, its value is left out of the computed accessible name. Example: a button whose aria-labelledby points to a hidden div that contains a text input with the value "Query" gets the name "Query". The same setup with an input of type search gives the button no name at all, so the button cannot be found by its role and name, and its ARIA snapshot shows only a nameless button. The same happens when the search input sits inside a label element: its value is dropped from the label text. Only the input type differs. Expected: the value of an embedded search input counts toward the name exactly as the value of an embedded text input does. In the accessible name computation rules, an embedded control that is a textbox contributes its value, and the searchbox role is a subclass of textbox. Playwright gives an input of type search the searchbox role. Other parts of Playwright's role handling already treat the two roles alike, for example for the read-only and disabled states. Seen on 1.63.0-next.
Search inputs embedded in a label or aria-labelledby target add nothing to the accessible name, unlike text inputs. Make them contribute their value too.

Running Playwright Test in the debug mode that hands a paused test over to the separate Playwright command-line tool breaks when a test uses more than one browser context. Setup: a worker-scoped fixture asks the shared browser for a new context, uses it, and closes it at teardown; the test itself also uses the built-in page. A normal test run passes. In the debug mode the run pauses at the start and prints a session name. After attaching to that session with the command-line tool and resuming, the test fails while the fixture creates its extra context, with an error saying that a browser server is already running. The cause: each time a context is created, the debug integration tries to expose the browser to the command-line tool again, and the second attempt throws. Expected: this debug mode works for tests that create several contexts; the browser is exposed once and all contexts keep working. Seen with Playwright Test 1.62, Node 22, Linux.
Debugging a test through the Playwright command-line tool crashes when the test creates a second browser context, for example in a worker-scoped fixture. Please make it work.

In Playwright 1.64 (development build), saving a browser context's storage state with IndexedDB included silently turns Map and Set values into empty plain objects. It happens the same way in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Steps: open a page, create an IndexedDB database with one object store, and put a Map with one entry ('mk' to 'mv') under the key 'map' and a Set of 1 and 2 under the key 'set'. Save the storage state with IndexedDB, create a new context from that state, and read both keys back. Both come back as empty plain objects, with no error or warning. The loss is already visible in the saved state, where both values are encoded as an object with no properties. Numbers, strings, dates, byte arrays, nested objects, bigint and undefined all survive the round trip. The serializer that encodes the snapshot has explicit cases for regular expressions, dates, URLs, errors, array buffers, typed arrays and bigint, but none for Map or Set. So both fall through to the generic object case, which walks only own enumerable properties. IndexedDB stores values with the structured clone algorithm, which supports Map and Set. Expected: after the restore, the Map and the Set come back as a Map and a Set with their contents. Scope: only the IndexedDB snapshot. A Map or Set returned from a page evaluation also becomes an empty object, but that is the documented serializable boundary for evaluation results. That is intentional and must stay as it is.
Saving storage state with IndexedDB turns stored Map and Set values into empty objects. Keep their contents through save and restore; don't change page evaluation results.

In Playwright, a locator that finds elements by role, with both an accessible name and a description, prints as the raw internal selector text instead of as the readable locator call when one of the two is a regular expression and the other is a plain string. For example, a button locator with a case-insensitive regular expression for the name and a plain string for the description should print as the role locator call with those two options. Instead it prints the internal role selector with the name and description in square brackets. The same happens with a plain string name and a regular expression description. The locator still matches, but this raw selector is what shows up in the locator line of assertion errors and in the call logs while waiting. The Python, Java and .NET versions print the raw selector too. Two regular expressions, or two strings, print fine. The cause is a recent check that the name and the description do not disagree on exact matching: a regular expression is parsed as case sensitive, so next to a string that is not exact it counts as a conflict. Seen from 1.61.0, still on main.
Role locators with a regex name and a plain string description, or the reverse, print as a raw internal selector instead of the readable locator. Please fix.

Playwright Test 1.63 added named locks: tests that hold the same lock do not run at the same time. Today a lock can be declared only in the details of a single test or of a titled test group. There is no way to declare a lock for the suite that is currently loading, from inside the file or group itself. Playwright Test already has a call that configures the enclosing file or group while tests are collected; it sets the execution mode, the retry count and the timeout. Please let that same call also accept a lock, given the same way as in test details, so that all tests in that file or group, including nested groups, take it. This must work together with a fixture override that is scoped to a group, so the lock covers only that group. Motivation: our tests choose a seed through a fixture override. Some seeds use a shared live third-party account, and those tests must not run at the same time. We wrap the fixture override so that a seed that needs the shared account also takes the lock. Today the only way is to reach into private internals of the suite that is loading. Shared or exclusive lock modes and typed lock names are out of scope.
Done when: the call that configures the enclosing group accepts a lock option, as one lock name or a list of names.

Let me declare a lock for the whole current test group from inside it, through the group configuration call that already sets execution mode, retry count and timeout.
Done when: the call that configures the enclosing group accepts a lock option, as one lock name or a list of names.

Playwright's clock control does not affect the Temporal API in the page. After a test fixes the page time to 1 January 2020 00:00 UTC and opens a blank page, a new Date reports that time, but the current instant from Temporal.Now still returns the real current time. This happens in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, which all ship Temporal natively. Expected: once Playwright controls time (by installing the fake clock, setting a fixed time or setting the system time), Temporal.Now always reports the same instant as Date. This covers every method of Temporal.Now that reads the clock: the current instant, and the current zoned date-time, plain date-time, plain date and plain time. The time zone lookup and the rest of the Temporal namespace stay untouched, so a method called without a time zone still uses the page's time zone. The fake clock already replaces Date, the timers, performance and date formatting, but not Temporal. Temporal.Now is the only part of Temporal that reads the clock. The fake timers library that Playwright's clock is derived from recently added the same support, in the same shape as its existing Intl replacement. Without this, code that moves from Date to Temporal silently runs against real time in tests. A Temporal polyfill hides the problem because it reads the current time from Date. Seen on Playwright 1.63.0.
Playwright's fake clock doesn't control Temporal.Now; it still returns real time. Make Temporal.Now follow the faked time like Date does.

Since Playwright 1.63 (a regression), highlighting a locator does nothing when the locator uses a custom selector engine that reads global variables of the page. Clicking the same locator works. Reproduction: in a worker-scoped automatic fixture, register a custom selector engine named 'tag' whose lookup functions return matching elements only when a flag variable on the window object is set, and nothing otherwise. The engine is registered without the option that runs it as an isolated content script. In a test, set that flag on the window from the page, set the page content to one button, create a locator with that engine for the button, and highlight it: nothing is highlighted. Clicking the locator then works. During the highlight the engine sees the flag as undefined, but during the click it sees it set. The reporter guesses that highlighting runs the selector in an isolated content script, although the engine was not registered for that. Real use case: a selector engine for UI5 apps that reads the UI5 API from a global object on the window; highlighting fails because that global is not defined. Expected: both highlighting and clicking work. Seen on 1.63.0, Windows 11.
Highlighting a locator that uses a custom selector engine relying on page globals stopped working in 1.63, though clicking it still works. Please fix.

When tracing is started with page snapshots turned on, Playwright calls on a page whose main thread is busy never finish, and even an explicit timeout on the call does not fire. Repro: start a local HTTP server, launch Chromium, create a context, start tracing with snapshots on, open a page and navigate to the server. Evaluate a script in the page that schedules an endless loop to start right after the script returns. Then navigate again with a 3-second timeout. With snapshots off, the evaluation returns at once and the navigation fails with a timeout error after about 3 seconds. With snapshots on, both calls stay pending (checked for 20 seconds; in CI a navigation with a 30-second timeout hung for more than 3 days). It happens every time on macOS and Linux, and also through the Python binding. Expected: tracing must not turn a bounded call into an unbounded one. Reporter's analysis: the steps that run before and after each call have a 3-second budget, but that budget can only cut off waits that are tied to it. The DOM snapshot capture waits on the page directly, so when the page never answers, the call never gets a response. A lint check meant to catch such untied waits misses this spot because the call uses optional chaining. Tying the snapshot wait to the budget, as the coverage capture already does, makes the repro finish.
With tracing snapshots on, Playwright calls on a page whose main thread is stuck hang forever and ignore their timeout. Make the timeout still apply.

In Playwright, when a browser context is created with JavaScript disabled, an action that has to retry, such as a click on a covered element, never finishes its wait between retries. Example: a page has a form button that a full-page overlay covers for 300 ms; a pure CSS animation hides the overlay, no script is involved. With JavaScript enabled, a click on the button succeeds after about 0.3 s. With JavaScript disabled, it takes about 30 s in the bundled Chromium headless shell, and in Google Chrome, headless or headed, it never completes and times out after 90 s. The cause: the short wait between action retries runs as a timer inside the page, and page timers do not run while script execution is disabled, even in the isolated world that Playwright uses for its own scripts. The promise stays pending until the browser garbage collects it, and Playwright then wrongly reports that the element was removed from the page. Animation frame callbacks still run, so the stability check works and only the retry wait hangs. The reporter proposes to do the retry wait on the Playwright side instead of in the page. Seen in 1.59.1 on macOS.
With JavaScript disabled in the browser context, a click that has to retry waits forever between retries. Make action retries work without page scripts.

In the Playwright MCP server, when the proxy is given on the command line, or through the matching environment variable, as a URL that contains a user name and password (user and password before an at sign, then host and port), the credentials are lost. The value is passed on only as the proxy server address. When that address is normalized, the user-info part of the URL is dropped, and the separate proxy user name and password fields stay empty. Against a proxy that needs authentication, navigating to a page then fails with an invalid-credentials network error, although no credentials were ever sent. Repro, offline: run a local proxy that answers 407 to any request without a proxy authorization header, start the MCP server over stdio with the proxy option pointing at it with credentials in the URL, and use the navigate tool to open any site. No authorization header reaches the proxy. The same proxy works when the server address, user name and password are set as separate fields in a config file, and a proxy without authentication works from the command line. The documentation does not say that only the config file works. Expected: when the command-line proxy value is parsed, take the user name and password from the URL, with percent-encoded characters decoded, put them into the proxy user name and password, and remove them from the server address. Playwright already authenticates from those fields. Seen with Playwright MCP 0.0.83, Chromium, Windows 10.
Playwright MCP ignores the user name and password written in the proxy URL given on the command line, so authenticated proxies fail. Use them, percent-decoded.

Playwright's API request context stores a cookie as already expired when its Set-Cookie header has Max-Age first and then an Expires date in the past. Example: a server sets a session id cookie with Max-Age of one hour, followed by Expires set to 1 January 1970 and path /. A later request does not send the cookie, so a server that echoes the cookie header gets an empty value. With the same two attributes in the other order, the cookie is kept. Expected: Max-Age takes precedence over Expires whatever the order of the attributes (RFC 6265 section 5.3), as in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, so the cookie lives one hour and is sent. Servers often send a past Expires next to Max-Age for old clients. Cause: the attributes are read in order and both set the same expiry, so the last one wins. A related problem: a Max-Age value that is not all digits, for example "10abc", is still read as a number; RFC 6265 section 5.2.2 says to ignore such an attribute. Seen on the main branch toward 1.64 and in 1.63; not platform-specific.
API request contexts drop a cookie when Max-Age comes before a past Expires. Max-Age should always win, and a Max-Age that is not a plain integer should be ignored.

Listing cookies for given URLs returns cookies that would not be sent to those URLs, and a cookie with path /foo/ is sent to /foo. Case 1: an API request context starts with a stored host-only cookie (domain example.com without a leading dot, path /api). Listing cookies for https://example.com/api/x returns it, which is right, but listing for https://sub.example.com/api/x and for https://example.com/apiv2 also returns it. Case 2: a server sets a cookie with path /foo/ on a response to /foo/set; a later request to /foo sends it. Expected, per the domain-match and path-match rules of RFC 6265 sections 5.1.3 and 5.1.4, which browsers follow and which the docs promise for browser contexts: a host-only cookie for example.com does not apply to sub.example.com, path /api does not apply to /apiv2, and path /foo/ does not apply to /foo. A path matches only exactly or on a slash boundary. Cause: the URL filter used for listing puts a dot in front of every cookie domain, so host-only cookies match all subdomains, and it compares paths as plain string prefixes. The API request context started to use this filter recently; before, it used the stricter check that decides what is sent. The same filter also serves cookie listing for browser contexts in all browsers, which report host-only cookies without a leading dot, so the bug likely exists there too. Separately, the path check used for sending adds a slash to the request path before it compares, so /foo matches /foo/. Seen on main toward 1.64 and in 1.63.
Fix cookie URL matching: listing cookies for a URL returns host-only cookies on subdomains and /api cookies on /apiv2, and a /foo/ cookie gets sent to /foo.

Regression on the development branch (1.65.0-next); it worked in 1.63. Playwright can turn an internal role selector into locator code for each supported language (JavaScript, Python, Java and C#), and can parse such locator code back into the selector. Take the role selector for a checkbox whose checked state is "mixed". The generated JavaScript locator asks for the checkbox role with the checked state set to the string 'mixed'. Parsing that code back now fails with an error that says the checked option is unexpected, instead of giving back the original selector. The same happens for the Python, Java and C# forms, and for the pressed state with the value "mixed". Expected: the round trip gives back the original selector, as it did before, because role matching supports "mixed" for the checked and pressed states. Cause: a recent change made the parser accept only true or false for every role option other than the name, so the string "mixed" is rejected. The problem does not depend on the operating system or the browser.
Parsing a role locator back to a selector fails when checked or pressed is set to 'mixed'. It worked before; please fix the regression.

On Playwright main (1.65 development build), turning locator code back into a selector fails for two locator methods that were added in 1.64: the method that scopes one locator to be inside another locator, and the page method that finds an element by its reference id from the page snapshot. The parser turns locator text, for example text pasted into the locator box of the trace viewer or the inspector, into a selector. Parsing a JavaScript locator for the third cell scoped inside a row locator throws an error that says the locator method is unsupported. Parsing a lookup by the reference id e5 throws the same error. So pasting the example from the documentation of the scoping method into the locator box does not resolve. Expected: the scoping call parses to the same selector that the client library produces for it (the outer locator, then a chained part with the inner locator), and the reference lookup parses to the same selector that the client produces for that call. This must work in all four languages (JavaScript, Python, Java and .NET), with each language's naming style for the two methods. Found by code review; not specific to an OS or browser.
The locator box in the trace viewer rejects the two locator methods added in 1.64 (scoping inside another locator, and lookup by snapshot reference). Support them in every language.

Playwright's MCP server, run over standard input and output, measured on Windows 11. When the client closes the server's standard input, two shutdown paths both run. First, when standard input ends, the server closes its transport, which closes the browser the normal way. Second, a separate exit handler reacts when standard input closes and starts the graceful close of all browsers. Both reach the graceful close of the same launched browser. The second call finds a close already in progress and force-kills the browser instead, 1 ms after the graceful close started. On Windows the force kill runs taskkill on the whole browser process tree through a shell. With browser debug logging on, the log shows the start of the graceful close, then a forced close and a force kill right after, then the process exit and the end of the graceful close, with Chromium and Firefox. With a persistent profile, the kill can land before the browser has written its stores: after a relaunch, one Chromium run lost a persistent cookie and one Firefox run lost every localStorage key of the page. Closing the browser with the MCP close tool before closing standard input kept everything. Expected: on standard input end the browser is closed once, gracefully, and force-killed only if that close does not finish. The reporter suggests letting a second graceful close wait for the first one, or giving the shutdown on standard input end a single owner.
When the MCP client closes the stdio server's input, Playwright force-kills the browser right after starting a graceful close and loses profile data. Close it once, gracefully.

Upgrading Playwright Test from 1.59.1 to 1.63.0 breaks a custom Node.js module loader that our config registers to compile MDX files imported by tests (the MDX project's Node.js loader, version 3.1.1, unchanged). Playwright now tries to parse the original MDX file as JavaScript itself, instead of letting the registered loader compile it, so listing the tests fails with a syntax error at the first Markdown heading and zero tests are collected. The cause is that Playwright moved to Node's synchronous module hooks, and Node runs synchronous hooks before asynchronous ones regardless of registration order, so Playwright's load hook sees the file first. Repro on Node.js 24: a config file that registers the MDX loader through Node's module registration API, an MDX file that exports a title and has a heading, and an ES module test file that imports the title and checks its value. Listing tests works on 1.59.1 and fails on 1.63.0. Request: for file extensions that Playwright does not transform itself, such as MDX, Playwright's load hook should pass the file on to the next loader in the chain before it reads or transforms the file, so that registered Node.js loaders can handle it. This keeps the existing Node.js loader API and adds no new Playwright API. Today's workarounds are to mark such files as external in Playwright's build settings, to force the old asynchronous loader mode with an environment variable, or to compile the files first. The test should be collected without any of these.
After upgrading Playwright, our registered Node.js loader for MDX imports is bypassed and test collection fails. Hand file types Playwright doesn't transform to registered loaders.

The Playwright MCP tool that lists the cookies of the browser context has an optional domain filter, and the filter matches by substring. This causes two problems. First, it returns cookies of unrelated domains: with cookies for example.com and my-example.com, filtering by example.com returns both, because the second name contains the first. So an agent or user who inspects one site gets cookies of other sites. Second, it misses matches: cookie domains are case-insensitive under RFC 6265, but a cookie set for example.com is not found when the filter is EXAMPLE.COM, and also not when the filter is .example.com with a leading dot. In both cases the tool reports that no cookies were found. Expected: the filter matches the exact domain and its subdomains, ignores case, and ignores a leading dot, like the cookie domain matching of RFC 6265 that Playwright already uses elsewhere. It does not match other domains that only contain the same text. Seen on the development branch (1.65.0-next).
The MCP cookie list's domain filter uses substring matching, so example.com also returns my-example.com cookies. Match the domain and its subdomains, case-insensitively.

On Playwright 1.65 (development build), filling an input of type datetime-local with a valid value that includes seconds, for example 2026-10-14T12:00:00 (a standard ISO timestamp cut to seconds), throws an error that says the value is not valid. The browser accepts the value, sets it, and stores it in normalized form: by the HTML specification for the datetime-local state, it drops the seconds when they are zero, so the input holds 2026-10-14T12:00. After it sets the value, Playwright compares the value that the input holds with the given text by strict equality, and raises the error when they differ. An earlier fix handled the same kind of problem for range inputs, which the browser also re-serializes. Expected: filling accepts the value, and the input holds the normalized value. Seen in Chromium and Firefox, on all platforms.
Filling a datetime-local input with seconds, like 2026-10-14T12:00:00, fails as an invalid value even though the browser accepts it. Please fix.

In Playwright, saving a browser context's storage state with IndexedDB included loses IndexedDB values and keys that are falsy: 0, false, the empty string and null. Example: a page opens a database with an object store that uses out-of-line keys (the layout that key-value wrappers like idb-keyval and localForage use) and stores count 0, enabled false, name as the empty string, deleted null and answer 42. After saving the state and restoring it into a new context, only answer comes back with its value; the other four come back as undefined, with no error. In the saved state, those records have no value field. A record with key 0 is saved with no key, so Playwright cannot load the state it just wrote: both creating a context from the saved state and setting the state on an existing context fail with an error that the object store has no key generator and no key was given. In a store with auto increment, a record with the explicit key 0 does not fail but is restored under a generated key. The same happens in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. The cause: when saving, the serialized value and key are checked for truthiness, so a falsy one is stored in neither form; when restoring, the check also turns a saved null into undefined. Both sides need a presence check. A related bug in the same code: every number is treated as JSON-safe, so Infinity is saved as null, both at the top level and nested inside objects. Expected: every record comes back with the key and value it was saved with. Seen in 1.64.1 and the 1.65 alpha.
Saving storage state with IndexedDB drops falsy values and keys like 0, false, empty string and null, and saves Infinity as null. Make the save and restore exact.

In Playwright with Chromium (seen on 1.59.1 and 1.64.1), the locale set on a browser context is not applied inside dedicated web workers. Repro: start a local HTTP server that logs the Accept-Language header of each request. Its main page fetches a URL that includes the page's navigator.languages and starts a dedicated worker; the worker script fetches a URL that includes the worker's navigator.languages. Launch Chromium, create a context with the locale set to German (Germany), open the page and wait a second. The requests for the page, from the page, and for the worker script all send German as Accept-Language, and the page sees German in navigator.languages. But the request made by the worker itself sends the browser's default English Accept-Language, and navigator.languages inside the worker is English. Expected: requests from inside the worker send the context locale as Accept-Language, and navigator.languages inside the worker matches the locale, like in the page. Context: a custom user agent already reaches dedicated workers, but the locale does not. When Playwright attaches to a new dedicated worker in Chromium, it does not send the browser protocol's user agent override, which also carries the accept-language value, to the worker's session. Sending that override with the locale to the worker's session fixes both the header and navigator.languages, as was done earlier for service workers.
In Chromium, the browser context locale is ignored inside dedicated web workers: their requests and language list stay English. Please make workers respect the locale.

pandas' testing helper that asserts two DataFrames are equal fails when a column MultiIndex has a missing value as a label. Example: a DataFrame has the columns Currency (all "USD"), Collateral (all None), Payment (dates 2023-01-01, 2023-01-01, 2023-02-01) and Cashflow (100.0, 100.0, 200.0). It is grouped by Currency, Collateral and Payment with missing keys kept, summed, the Currency and Collateral levels are moved from the row index to the columns, and the top column level is dropped. The result has one column labeled ("USD", NaN) and the two Payment dates as rows, each with the value 200.0. The reporter first built the expected column index from tuples; then the Collateral level had the object dtype instead of float64, and the helper reported a dtype difference. Next they built it from a "USD" level named Currency and a float64 level holding None named Collateral. The comparison still fails: the helper reports that the column names differ and shows ('USD', nan) on both sides. The helper treats missing values as equal when a name is a single value, but not when the missing value sits inside a tuple. Expected: the comparison passes, because missing values nested in tuple labels should count as equal.
pandas' DataFrame equality assertion fails when a MultiIndex column label contains NaN, though both labels look identical. Make missing values inside tuple labels compare equal.

In pandas, extracting regular-expression capture groups into columns fails for a string Series whose dtype is the generic Arrow-backed dtype built directly from a pyarrow string type. It works only when every capture group is named. Take a Series of "a1" and "b2" with that dtype and a pattern of a letter a or b followed by a digit, each in its own group. (1) Both groups named (for example 'letter' and 'digit'): correct. (2) No group named: raises an error that the pattern must contain a named group. (3) A named group 'letter' followed by an unnamed group: pyarrow raises an error that the regular expression contains unnamed groups. (4) The same mixed pattern with a regex flag such as ignore-case (on main only): no error, but the column of the unnamed group is all missing values, while it still gets its label. The same calls work on object dtype, on the default string dtype, and on the pandas string dtype with pyarrow storage. The public method rejects only patterns with zero capture groups, so an unnamed group is valid, and the method's own documentation example extracts an unnamed group into column 0. Expected: the same result for all dtypes. Unnamed groups are labelled by their position, named groups by their name, and the two kinds can be mixed, with the same labels that the other dtypes already produce. For example, no named groups gives columns 0 and 1, and the mixed pattern gives columns 'letter' and 1. The reporter notes that this code path already has an element-by-element fallback with Python's regex module for the cases that the pyarrow kernel cannot serve (a regex flag, a compiled pattern); patterns with an unnamed group could take that fallback and be labelled by position.
Extracting regex capture groups from a generic Arrow-backed string Series fails or drops columns when groups are unnamed. Label unnamed groups by position, like other dtypes.

In pandas, converting a Series of intervals whose bounds are timezone-aware datetimes to a pyarrow array fails. Example: make intervals from the breaks of a date range of five days from 2012 with the timezone Europe/Brussels, put them in a Series, and pass the Series to pyarrow's array function. It raises a type error that says this interval subtype cannot be converted. The conversion looks up the arrow type of the interval subtype with pyarrow's lookup for numpy types, which fails for every pandas extension type as subtype, also for the timezone-aware datetime type, which intervals otherwise support. Reading such interval data from arrow was fixed earlier, but writing still fails. Only allowing the write is not enough: pandas' registered arrow extension type for intervals stores the subtype as text in its metadata and reads it back with pyarrow's lookup of type names, which has no name for a timezone-aware timestamp. So a parquet file written that way fails to read back with an error that there is no type alias for that timestamp. Expected: the conversion to pyarrow works for a timezone-aware interval subtype, and the result round-trips through parquet back to the same interval dtype.
Converting pandas intervals with timezone-aware datetime bounds to pyarrow fails. Make it work, and make it round-trip through parquet back to the same dtype.

A group-by on two or more keys, where at least one key is a categorical column, with group sorting turned off and unobserved categories included, maps group labels to the wrong rows. Example: a frame with an integer column with values 0, 1 and 2, and an ordered categorical column with categories "low" then "mid", where the rows for each integer come in the order mid, low. So the order of first appearance differs from the category order. Group by both columns. The group-by attribute that maps each group label to its row positions gives the labels in category order but the row groups in first-appearance order, and pairs them, so each label points at the rows of another group. Fetching one group by its label, for example (0, "low"), relies on that mapping and silently returns the rows of another group. The other attribute, which maps each group label to its row labels, is correct, so the two disagree for the same group-by object. A popular plotting library groups this way, so its faceted plots draw each facet's data under another facet's title. Expected: fetching a group returns the rows that hold that label, and the two mappings agree.
Grouping by several keys including a categorical one, without sorting and keeping unobserved categories, pairs group labels with the wrong rows, so fetching a group returns another group's rows.

In an as-of merge (a merge on the nearest key), the setting for the largest allowed distance between matching keys accepts zero. Zero is meaningful: it allows exact key matches only. Example: left keys 1, 5 and 10, right keys 1, 6 and 10, and a distance limit of 0 give matches for 1 and 10 and a missing value for 5. A negative limit is correctly rejected with a merge error, but the error text says that the limit has to be positive, which wrongly suggests that zero is invalid too. The checks for time-delta keys, integer keys and float keys all reject only values below zero, so the text disagrees with what they accept. Expected: the error for a negative limit says that the limit must be non-negative, for every key type, and zero stays accepted.
The as-of merge error for a negative distance limit says it has to be positive, but zero is allowed. Make the message say non-negative.

In pandas, the incremental mode of the exponentially weighted mean, the one that can later be fed new rows, gives wrong results for a DataFrame with a single column: it ignores the decay and returns the plain cumulative mean. Example: a one-column DataFrame with values 1, 2, 3, 4 and a center of mass of 1. The normal exponentially weighted mean gives 1.0, 1.667, 2.429, 3.267, but the incremental mode gives 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5. Feeding a new row with value 5 to the incremental mode afterwards is wrong in the same way: it gives 3.0 instead of about 4.161. A Series and frames with two or more columns happen to give correct results, which is why this went unnoticed. The reporter found two mistakes that combine. First, the array of time steps between observations is sized from the number of columns instead of the number of rows. Second, the numba-compiled kernel reads that array with the column position instead of the row position, although the comment next to it says the array is meant per row. For a single column the array is empty, the out-of-range read returns 0, and the old weight never decays. This has been wrong since the incremental mode was added in pandas 1.3.0. Expected: the incremental mode agrees with the normal exponentially weighted mean for any number of columns.
The incremental exponentially weighted mean in pandas ignores the decay for single-column DataFrames and returns a plain cumulative mean. Please make it match the normal one.

Converting a pandas Categorical of date strings to datetime values gives a different container type depending on its length. With 50 copies of the same timestamp string, the conversion returns a datetime index. With 51 copies, it returns a categorical index instead. A categorical index does not support datetime operations such as timezone localization or formatting as strings. Because the type switches with the size of the input, code behaves differently on small data, for example in unit tests, and on large data in production. The result type should be the same whatever the input size.
Converting a categorical of date strings to datetime values returns a categorical index once it has more than 50 values; it should always return datetime values.

pandas' equality assertions for Series and DataFrames crash with a TypeError instead of raising the normal assertion error when an object-dtype column holds lists with different nesting. Example: one Series of object dtype holds 1, the list [1, 2], and "b"; a second holds 1, the list [1, 2, 3], and "b". Comparing them gives the expected assertion error: it says that the values of the two Series differ, gives the share of values that differ (33.33333 %), shows both sides, and names the earliest position that differs, position 1, with [1, 2] against [1, 2, 3]. But when the second Series holds the nested list [[1, 2]] in place of [1, 2, 3], the comparison raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' from the low-level element comparison. The same happens for DataFrames. Expected: the same kind of assertion error as for the flat lists, with the share of values that differ and the earliest position that differs.
pandas' Series/DataFrame equality assertion crashes with an unhashable-list TypeError when object columns hold lists of different nesting. It should raise a normal assertion failure.

In pandas, a group-by aggregation over two keys gives a result with a two-level row index, and its display in an IPython (Jupyter) notebook is wrong when the first key holds distinct float values that look the same after formatting. Example: an id column of the 10 distinct floats 201500000100 to 201500000109, each repeated three times, a column of random integers, and a letter column that cycles A, B, C. Grouping by id alone and summing gives 10 rows, each labelled 2.015000e+11, which is correct. Grouping by id and the letter column and summing shows the first-level label 2.015000e+11 only once at the top, with blanks below it for all 30 rows. So the table looks like a single id with A, B, C repeated ten times, instead of ten separate ids with three rows each. Converting the id to strings before grouping gives a table that looks correct. Expected: the display does not show different first-level values as one group only because their printed text is the same. Reported on pandas 0.16.2, Python 2.7, Windows.
A table with a two-level row index shows distinct labels as one merged group when they print identically, like large floats shown as 2.015000e+11. Please fix.

In pandas, group-by cumulative sum, cumulative minimum, cumulative maximum and rank give wrong results on datetime or timedelta columns when a group key is NaN, with the default setting that drops rows whose key is missing. There is no warning. Example: a DataFrame with a key column 0, 0, NaN, 0 and a timedelta column 1 hour, missing, 2 hours, 3 hours, grouped by the key, on the timedelta column. The cumulative sum gives huge negative timedeltas in the second and fourth rows. The cumulative minimum gives missing in the fourth row. The cumulative maximum gives 1 hour in the second row instead of missing. Rank gives 2, 1, NaN, 3. Expected: the same result as if the NaN-key rows were not there, and missing values (NaN for rank) in the NaN-key rows: cumulative sum 1 h, missing, missing, 4 h; cumulative minimum 1 h, missing, missing, 1 h; cumulative maximum 1 h, missing, missing, 3 h; rank 1, NaN, NaN, 2. Nanosecond precision is also lost: for two datetimes at 1 and 2 nanoseconds after midnight with keys 0 and NaN, the cumulative maximum of the first row drops the nanosecond. Without a NaN key the results are correct. The cause: for transforms where some keys were dropped, integer values are cast to 64-bit float so that the dropped rows can be filled with NaN. Datetime and timedelta values are viewed as 64-bit integers before that point, so they are cast too. After the cast the missing-datetime marker is an ordinary large negative number, so it is no longer treated as missing, and values above 2**53 are rounded. The same problem was fixed earlier for nullable integer types, but not for datetime and timedelta. A possible fix: do not cast datetime and timedelta values to float, and fill the output of the dropped rows with the missing-datetime value instead.
Group-by cumulative sum, min, max and rank on datetime or timedelta columns mishandle missing values and lose nanosecond precision when a group key is NaN. Please fix.

In pandas 3.0.3, reading an Excel workbook with a two-row column header and the first column as the index fails, while reading the same data from a CSV file with the same options works. The reporter has the same small table as a CSV file and as an xlsx workbook. Reading the CSV with the first two rows as a multi-level column header and the first column as the index returns an empty DataFrame, with no columns and no rows. Reading the workbook with the same options and the openpyxl engine raises a value error that says one name was expected but two were given, for sheet 0. Expected: no error, and the Excel read gives the same result as the CSV read.
pandas raises an error when reading an Excel file with a two-row header and the first column as index, where the same CSV gives an empty DataFrame. Please fix.

When pandas reads a SAS data file in the sas7bdat format, rows that were deleted in SAS are still returned. The reporter filled a table in SAS with five rows of date and datetime values, then deleted two of the rows, the third and the fifth. SAS keeps deleted rows in the file and only marks them as deleted. pandas reads all five rows, and the deleted rows show up with missing or default values. Expected: a DataFrame with only the three rows that were not deleted, without the third and the fifth row.
Reading a sas7bdat file into pandas returns rows that were deleted in SAS. Skip the deleted rows.

In pandas 1.1.0, reading a JSON file that contains only {"file_path": null} as a Series (not as a DataFrame), and then converting the result to a dictionary, gives the missing datetime value NaT for that key. The user expected an ordinary missing value (they expected None), because nothing in the data suggests a date. Why is a JSON null turned into a datetime missing value instead?
Reading a JSON object with only a null value as a Series turns the null into NaT; it should stay an ordinary missing value.

In pandas, limiting the values of a Series of ordered categorical data to a range, with both a lower and an upper bound, gives the wrong result. Example: a categorical Series with the values zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, with its categories reordered to zero < one < two < three < four < five < six and marked as ordered. Limiting with only a lower bound of two, or only an upper bound of four, gives the expected output. Limiting with lower bound two and upper bound four gives four, four, four, two, two, two, two instead of the expected two, two, two, three, four, four, four, with the same ordered categorical dtype. Swapping the two bounds does not change the result. The likely cause: when both bounds are scalars, the method puts them in order with the plain minimum and maximum of the two values, which here is alphabetical string order, not the order of the categories.
Limiting an ordered categorical Series to a lower and upper bound gives wrong values; the bounds get ordered by value instead of by category order. Please fix.

In pandas 3.1.0rc0 and on the main branch, appending a DataFrame with a categorical column to an HDF5 store in table format fails with the wrong error when the stored data has integer categories and the new data has float categories. Steps: make a DataFrame with one categorical column of the integers 1, 2, 3, 1 (categories 1, 2, 3), and a second one with the same column as the floats 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 1.0 (categories 1.0, 2.0, 4.0). Open a new HDF5 store, append the first frame in table format under a key, then append the second frame under the same key. In pandas 3.0.6 the second append is rejected with the intended value error, which says that the new categories differ from the stored ones, so the data cannot be appended. Now it fails inside compiled code instead, with a value error about a buffer type mismatch (expected double, got long). Expected: the second append raises the same different-categories error as in 3.0.6.
Appending float categories to integer categories in an HDF5 table now fails with a low-level buffer type error instead of the different-categories error. Please restore it.

On a DataFrame, forward fill and backward fill of missing values ignore the request to work in place when they run along the columns (axis 1, or the string for columns). Example: a one-row DataFrame with columns A, B and C and the values 1.0, NaN and 3.0. Forward or backward filling it along the columns in place leaves the original DataFrame unchanged and returns a separate DataFrame that holds the filled values, so the returned object is not the original. Along the rows (axis omitted, 0, or the string for index) both methods work: they change the original and return it. Since pandas 3.0, these methods return the object itself, not None, when they work in place. The reporter traced the cause: for the column direction, the shared fill code transposes the DataFrame, fills it, transposes it back and returns that result at once. This skips the later step that applies an in-place result to the original. Under Copy-on-Write, filling the derived object does not change the original. Seen with pandas 3.0.6 and the 3.2 development version. Expected: when asked to work in place, both methods change the original DataFrame and return that same object.
Forward/backward filling a DataFrame in place along the columns leaves it unchanged and returns a copy. Make it modify and return the original.

In pandas 0.21, building a DataFrame from a list of records ignores the option that lists columns to leave out when the label to leave out is 0. With the records [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] and [7, 8, 9], and the first column (label 0) used as the index, the result still has the columns 0, 1 and 2, both when column 0 is also listed to be left out and when it is not. With the second column (label 1) used as the index, or with label 1 listed to be left out, the columns are correctly 0 and 2. The reporter found the cause: a check on the set of labels to leave out is true only when some label is truthy, so a label of 0 counts as false and nothing is dropped. Checking only whether the set is non-empty fixes it for them.
Building a DataFrame from records keeps a column that should be left out, or that became the index, when its label is 0. Please fix that.
